In the circuit shown in the figure, the resistances of the three resistors are $R_{1}=2\Omega$, $R_{2}=3\Omega$, $R_{3}=4\Omega$, and the voltage of the power supply is constant.

1. When switch $S$ is turned on and switch $S^{\prime}$ is turned off, what is the ratio of the voltages across $R_{1}$ and $R_{2}$?
2. When both switches $S$ and $S^{\prime}$ are turned on, what is the ratio of the voltages across $R_{1}$ and $R_{2}$?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure shows a circuit with the power supply labeled U at the bottom. Switch S is on the lower/right part of the main circuit and controls whether the source is connected. Resistor R1 is on the left side before a junction. From that junction to the right-side node there are two branches: the upper branch contains R2, and the lower branch contains R3 in series with switch S′. Therefore, when S′ is open, the R3 branch is disconnected; when S′ is closed, R2 and R3 connect between the same two nodes and are parallel. Reasoning: Given R1 = 2 Ω, R2 = 3 Ω, R3 = 4 Ω. 1. With S closed and S′ open, the lower branch containing R3 is broken, so the conducting circuit has only R1 and R2 in series. In series, the same current flows through both resistors, so the voltage ratio equals the resistance ratio: U1/U2 = R1/R2 = 2/3. 2. With both S and S′ closed, R2 and R3 are parallel, and this parallel combination is in series with R1. The equivalent resistance of R2 and R3 is R23 = (R2 R3)/(R2 + R3) = (3 × 4)/(3 + 4) = 12/7 Ω. The voltage across R2 is the same as the voltage across the entire parallel combination. Since R1 is in series with this parallel equivalent, the ratio of the voltage across R1 to the voltage across R2 is U1/U2 = R1/R23 = 2/(12/7) = 7/6.

Resistor R1 is on the left side before a junction. From that junction to the right-side node there are two branches: the upper branch contains R2, and the lower branch contains R3 in series with switch S′. Therefore, when S′ is open, the R3 branch is disconnected; when S′ is closed, R2 and R3 connect between the same two nodes and are parallel.

Reasoning: Given R1 = 2 Ω, R2 = 3 Ω, R3 = 4 Ω.

The voltage across R2 is the same as the voltage across the entire parallel combination. Since R1 is in series with this parallel equivalent, the ratio of the voltage across R1 to the voltage across R2 is U1/U2 = R1/R23 = 2/(12/7) = 7/6.
